newsitem.title: USA: Port of Miami audits repeatedly noted losses.
newsitem.headline: Port of Miami audits repeatedly noted losses.

text.p: Auditors for Port of Miami said Wednesday that they had repeatedly warned in their annnual reports and management letters that the seaport had operating losses and a large number of uncollected debts.

"The applicable numbers were disclosed year in and year out," Ron Jones, an auditor at Deloitte & Touche, told the Dade County Commission's maritime trade committee. "The information has been presented. It certainly hasn't shown any optimistic portrayal of anything."

Commissioners for Dade County, which runs the port, called the auditors in Wednesday to question why the commission only learned last week that the port has a $22 million cash flow deficit and that it had borrowed $37 million from the county general fund over several years to keep operating.
"The auditors have to sound a loud bell at the smell of a rat," Commissioner Miriam Alonso said. "In this case the rat has been dead a long time."

But the auditors pointed to the annual reports they submitted to the county. The reports showed the seaport had operating losses in seven of the last 10 years, with the annual losses ranging from $840,000 to $7.8 million.
Several of their management letters noted that many seaport customers routinely failed to pay their bills within 90 days and urged the port to adopt tougher collections procedures.

Every year, the seaport responded, "We agree with the observations," and said that it had trouble collecting accounts receivable during times of economic difficulty, another Deloitte auditor, Susan Tripp, told the commmission.
Alonso also questioned why the auditors had not previously asked to review the records of Fiscal Operations Inc, the company that operates the seaport's cargo cranes.
Tripp and Jones said it was because port Director Carmen Lunetta had approved Fiscal Operations' budgets and that the company was regularly audited by another accounting firm.

She said Deloitte asked for the records this year because auditors thought it odd that cargo revenues had dropped when additional cranes had been added, and because media reports had rased questions about the company's spending.

Lunetta, 67, abruptly announced his retirement after the Fiscal Operations' records were released. Alonso also confirmed Wednesday that the U.S. Attorney's Office is investigating Fiscal Operations' relationship with Lunetta and the port.
County manager Armando Vidal said county attorneys were reviewing the contract with Fiscal Operations.
Asked whether he and other county officials should have realized earlier that the seaport was in the red, Vidal said "I don't think finger pointing is the issue."
He said the county is taking "a new, fresh look" at seaport operations and instituting tighter controls.
